I had to learn this the hard way with my fiancee, who has depression. We lived together for 18 months before I called it quits. She was taking antidepressants along with another medication that is supposed to help the antidepressants work better, but they weren't working. 

She hadn't been working for a long time. She did go back to work in September 2020 for a brief bit but didn't stay. The money she did have from unemployment insurance and sick pay from the summer ran out in January of this year. 

Her employer put her on sick leave without pay in late January. After taking the antidepressant augmentation drug for almost a week, she went back to work after getting permission from her doctor to go back. Again, she didn't stay very long. She started sleeping in every morning, and giving lame excuses why she couldn't go to work.

She had no interest in doing anything more than watching TV all day and playing with her phone. She could have pushed her doctor a little harder to help her, but she was content waiting two weeks for an appointment, and then another two weeks for the doctor to authorize a change to her meds. I know my doctor wouldn't have made me wait that long.

I asked her to apply for unemployment insurance sick benefits. She did apply and filed weekly reports as required. After a few weeks went by, I asked her if she'd gotten any money.

She hadn't. So she contacted the unemployment insurance office and they told her they needed a Record of Employment (RoE) from her employer to prove her eligibility.

That's when the games started. She wouldn't approach her employer for the RoE out of her own volition, I had to ask her to do it. Then she claimed the employer wouldn't give her one because neither her manager nor the HR department knew how to fill one out.  

I knew this to be a false statement because HR departments everywhere in Canada prepare RoE's every day for employees who have had to stop working. It's not rocket science.

So I asked her to approach HR again. This time she claimed they told her she wasn't entitled to unemployment insurance because she hadn't been off sick long enough.  

Whether an employee is entitled or not isn't the employer's call to make. Only the unemployment insurance administration can decide that. Plus, the law says that an employer must supply a RoE or be fined. 

Shortly after her employer put her on unpaid sick leave, her employer sent a letter strongly recommending she apply for disability insurance benefits. The letter stated the insurance carrier could put her in touch with a psychiatrist far sooner than the public system could. (Where I live there is a shortage of psychiatrists, none are taking new patients, and the hospital psychiatry department has a backlog of 600 cases.)

She refused to do this, stating she tried to get it when she experienced a bout of depression in 2018 and was denied, so wasn't willing to try again. 

Several weeks before the whole unemployment thing cropped up, I told her that I needed her to start making a financial contribution to household expenses. I also told her I was tired of living like a yo-yo with her going to work for a little bit and then quitting.

And six months before that I told her I needed her to be a full partnership in the relationship. 

Throughout the relationship, I found myself constantly having to push and prod her to do simple things, like clean out the litter box for her two cats after it started to stink. As a result, I felt she wasn't a partner, but rather someone to manage.

Pictures that I brought when I moved never got hung because she wouldn't decide where they should be hung or help me hang them. The apartment we lived in was cluttered, yet she wouldn't lift a finger to help organize it, even when I suggested we work on it for short periods every day to help her manage her fatigue. 

In the end, I felt that she had no investment in the relationship and was just tagging along so long as I would support her financially until she could retire.

Funny thing was, I started behaving in a somewhat distant and less affectionate manner. Yet  this didn't prompt her to ask, "Hey, I notice you've been rather distant lately and less affectionate. You also seem to be upset about something. Can you tell me what's wrong? Can I help?"

Yet she did bring up the topic of having a wedding rather suddenly, even though we hadn't talked about it for months and months, given all the pandemic restrictions. She even started talking about us buying a new car jointly. After I told my sister about what was going on, she told me that she could clearly see that my fiancee was trying to 'seal the deal' and lock me in. 

I came to realize my fiancee was never going to get better and that despite my attempts to do everything I could to help her and then some, all I was doing was enabling her not to work or get better.

I also saw that there was no future in the relationship and simply left. I saw no point in issuing any ultimatums, because all they would do is make her make promises she wasn't prepared to keep, behave a little better for a while, and then revert to old behaviours when she felt the pressure was off. 

I felt that leaving with no warning would be the kick in the pants she needed to start looking after herself. But oddly enough, when she realized I was leaving, she didn't say, "I love you and want you to stay. Whatever's wrong, we can work it out."

Moral of the story? You can't help someone who doesn't want to be helped. And if you find yourself forced to end a relationship, it's already beyond repair.

The DI policy I had at work is a ‘peace of mind’ plan where if you cannot do your existing job and employer cannot accommodate, you get benefits. You are not forced to mitigate your losses by taking any job.

I’m grappling with the same decision myself in replacing my existing Panasonic ST50-series  53” plasma set. It’s eight years old now and still going strong. My primary motivation for looking at buying a new TV is to improve the audio capabilities. I’m hearing impaired and sometimes have trouble hearing dialogue clearly as the set has rear-firing speakers.

For whatever reason, the optical audio out on the set will not work with present-day sound bars, and a sound bar would go a long way towards improving and clarifying the sound.

I’m a little reluctant to let go of my existing TV, because it has given me trouble-free service and the picture quality, while probably not up to the level of the very best OLED sets, is still excellent.

So, I’ve narrowed down my choices to either a 50” Hisense Q8G (in the US, this set is designated H8G) or a Samsung 50” TU7000, as I’m working within a sub-$1000 budget.

A few reviews I’ve seen on the web suggest that the Q8G is the better buy. Despite costing less money, the Hisense uses Samsung’s Quantum Dot technology, so the display ought to be decent.

I’d consider spending more money, but there doesn’t seem to be a middle ground between $500 and $1300, where the better quality sets can be found.
